lesson.title: Getting Past the Router: The NAT Traversal Problem
lesson.summary: When two devices each sit behind their own NAT, as most devices on the internet do, neither one has a public address the other can simply connect to, which is exactly the obstacle peer-to-peer connections have to overcome.
lesson.body:
A NAT device, most home and office routers, sits between a private network and the public internet and rewrites addresses so that many devices on the private side can share one public IP address. From the outside, the internet only sees the NAT's public IP and whatever port it happens to be using for a given connection, the private device's actual address is never visible externally. This works fine for the ordinary client-server pattern most applications are built around. A client behind a NAT initiates an outbound connection, the NAT creates a mapping for it on the fly, tracking which internal address and port that outbound packet came from so it knows where to route the replies, and the reply traffic comes back through that mapping without issue, because the NAT is already expecting it.

The trouble starts the moment a connection has to go the other direction, an unsolicited inbound connection to a device behind a NAT, which is exactly what peer-to-peer connections need, since neither participant is a well-known server sitting at a fixed, reachable address. If a peer behind NAT A tries to connect to a peer behind NAT B out of nowhere, NAT B has no existing mapping for that traffic. As far as it is concerned, an unsolicited packet has arrived addressed to its public IP with no record of any internal host having asked for it, and it is dropped. This is not a bug, it is exactly what NAT is supposed to do with unsolicited traffic, and it is the same behavior that protects private networks from random inbound connections generally. But it means two ordinary devices, each behind its own separate home router, genuinely cannot just dial each other directly the way a client dials a public server, even though both devices might be perfectly willing to talk to each other.

A widely used technique for getting around this, when it works, is called hole punching. If both peers can be told about each other's public IP and port, learned via a third party both can reach, which is exactly what STUN provides, covered next, and both peers simultaneously send outbound traffic toward each other's public address, each NAT sees what looks like an outbound connection originating from its own side and creates a mapping for it, right around the time the other side's inbound packet arrives. If the timing lines up, each NAT ends up treating the other side's packet as a reply to its own outbound one, and a direct path opens up. This does not work against every kind of NAT. Some NAT implementations, often called symmetric NATs, assign a different public port for every destination a device talks to, which defeats the trick, because the port learned from talking to a third party will not be the same port used to reach the actual peer. That failure case is exactly why a fallback beyond hole punching, relaying through TURN, still needs to exist, which is the subject of the next chapter.
